routes.h1: A forecast you can check, not just read
routes.standfirst: HazardNet is an independent, open research platform that turns satellite observations and weather forecasts into continuous 15-day daily outlooks for eight climate hazards across Bangladesh’s 64 districts. Every figure it shows comes from a named artifact with a build date, the validation scorecard is published whether it flatters the model or not, and the boundary between this platform and the agencies that issue official warnings is stated on every page.

sections.h2: Start here: what to do with an outlook
paragraphs: Use an outlook as lead time, in this order: find your district, read the hazard, the 15-day daily trajectory, the peak severe date, the severity index and the confidence together, then check the official bulletin for that hazard before you act. The sections below explain each of those pieces; the links here are the working surfaces.
bullets: For a farm decision (planting, spraying, irrigating or harvesting), a district outlook tells you when to pay attention, not what to do in a particular field. Confirm the step locally, with extension advice where you can.

For an extension or union parishad decision, start from the published alerts and the sector advisories: each alert carries its evidence and policy version, and each advisory names the issuing authority at each step.
For a research or review question, start from the validation scorecard and the model card rather than from a colour on the map: they state what was checked, and what the counts cannot support.
In an emergency, do not act on this page. Call 999, and follow your local administration and the official BMD or FFWC bulletin over anything published here.

sections.h2: What HazardNet is for, and who it serves
paragraphs: The operational question in Bangladesh agriculture is rarely whether a hazard is coming; it is which districts, at which crop stage, with how many days of lead time, and how much weight the number deserves. HazardNet is built to answer that second set of questions. For each district across all 15 consecutive days it publishes a hazard class, a severity index, peak severe dates, a confidence bin and an independent physics estimate: and the run they came from.

It is written for three readers at once: farmers and rural residents checking the outlook for their own district before planting, spraying, irrigating or harvesting; agricultural extension workers and union parishad officials deciding whom to warn and what to prepare; and researchers and reviewers judging whether a published number deserves the weight it asks for.
bullets: 64 districts on the live map; the published advisory archive covers 507 ADM3 units (495 upazilas plus 12 city corporations).
Eight hazard classes: cold wave, drought, fire, flash flood, flood, heat wave, severe local storm and tropical cyclone.
The aim is a better district-level decision, on a farm, in a parishad office or in a review, made knowing exactly how much to trust the number. It is not a replacement for an official warning.

sections.h2: The current outlook, and where to see it
paragraphs: This page is the record; the live map is the outlook. The split is deliberate and documented, because the two questions need different pages: "where is the hazard now" is answered by a map, and "who produced this, from what, and how would I know if it stopped working" is answered by a document with dates on it.

The strip under the headline reads the committed alert artifact on every load: how many alerts are published at each level, how many districts the last run covered, and how many assessed rows the publication gate withheld. When nothing is published it says so, and says why: silence on a hazard platform is read as safety, so this page does not leave that to be inferred.
bullets: The live map addresses all 64 districts. A district the current run does not cover keeps its static baseline colour and says so on its own page, rather than borrowing a neighbour's number.

Every published alert carries its own evidence: the drivers behind the level, the policy version applied, and whether a duty officer reviewed it or the engine published it on its own at or below its configured ceiling.
The status page carries the age of every artifact this deployment ships, measured against the SLO it is held to, together with the notes each run reports against itself.

sections.h2: What a forecast is, and how it differs from an alert
paragraphs: Every forecast on HazardNet is a published record: one district, a continuous 15-day daily sequence (Days 1 to 15), a dominant hazard class, a continuous severity index (0 to 100), peak severe dates, and a confidence score, stamped with the date of the run that produced it. No forecast, alert or figure on this site is produced by a language model: every number is read from a committed artifact, and no number is interpolated to fill a gap in a run.

An alert is narrower than a forecast. It is a forecast row the publication gate has released as a card, with its level, evidence, policy version and reviewer state attached. A district can therefore have a forecast on the map while no alert is published for it; and, as the strip under the headline states, no published alert is not the same as no hazard.
bullets: Results only: how a record is generated is research-private and is not published.
Every figure on this site traces to a published forecast record with a forecast date.
Two severity tracks are reported per record, a skill track and a physics track, each shown with its own honest label.
Each daily run covers 15 consecutive forecast dates (Days 1 to 15), highlighting peak severe dates across the full window; Days 8 to 15 carry greater meteorological uncertainty than Days 1 to 7.

sections.h2: Severity, alert levels and confidence are three different things
paragraphs: A forecast record carries three values that are easy to merge into one impression of danger. Severity is the continuous value recorded for one district, hazard class and forecast date across the 15-day sequence. The alert level is the published tier a released alert carries. Confidence is neither of those: it is an uncalibrated model score (a softmax output), not a probability that the event will happen, and it should always be read beside the severity value and the forecast date.
bullets: No alert: nothing unusual for the season in the published alert record. On forecast records the lowest advisory tier is named NORMAL; the two labels belong to two related lists, and neither is a promise that a district is safe.
Watch (monitor): conditions are favourable for a hazard.
Warning (prepare): a damaging event is plausible.
Severe (act): an event is imminent or likely. What action is safe is set by the official bulletin and your local administration, not by this platform.
A level is carried as a word as well as a colour, so it stays readable in glare, and for readers who cannot rely on colour alone.

callout.text: These are HazardNet's decision-support tiers. They are not BMD cyclone signals, FFWC flood bulletins or evacuation instructions, and an official bulletin outranks them wherever the two differ.

sections.h2: How it works, and when it updates
paragraphs: Each run publishes dated data files. This site calls them artifacts. The live map, the alert cards, the status page and this front door all read the same files, so any figure can be followed back to the file and forecast date behind it instead of being taken on trust from a page design.

Forecasts are updated in daily runs, so freshness is something you can check rather than assume: the strip under the headline gives the alerts file's age at the moment of this read, every forecast record carries its forecast date, and the status page states each artifact's age against the limit (its SLO) it is held to.
bullets: What is published here is the result, and the evidence needed to check it. How a record is generated (model code, dataset collection and training) is research-private and is not described on this site.
No forecast, alert or figure on this site is produced by a language model, and no number is interpolated to fill a gap in a run.
A district a run did not cover says so on its own page. It does not borrow a neighbour's number, and it is not shown as zero.

sections.h2: Validation, and how to check any number on this site
paragraphs: A claim that cannot be checked is marketing. The platform therefore publishes the evidence next to the claim, including the places where the evidence is thin.
bullets: The status page reads the committed artifacts and states the age of each against its SLO: including when a source is stale, failing or unprovenanced, which is the case the page exists to show.
The validation scorecard reports per-episode detection counts for five historical episodes and states plainly what those numbers cannot support.

The model card lists the known failure modes and the out-of-scope uses, and carries the 2,931-event training claim as reported rather than verified: that archive is not redistributed by this repository, and the pages that would need it say it is absent instead of quoting the figure as if it had been read.
The code, the artifacts and the build scripts are in one public repository, and this site is rebuilt from them: the same pipeline that publishes a number also publishes the check on it.

sections.h2: Access, languages, and when something is missing
paragraphs: HazardNet is free and non-commercial on the web, and the map and the published record need no account. The app installs as a PWA, a web app you can add to a phone's home screen. It caches its tiles and keeps working when the connection does not. The pages are built for low-end Android phones, slow or metered connections and reading in sunlight, and the download centre carries the forecast snapshot and the offline builds for use away from a connection. Printed district briefs are a first-class output, not an afterthought.

Bangla and English sit side by side. The switch at the top of this page renders the front door's editorial copy and its controls in Bengali; the alert cards, the map and the district tables were translated first. The long-form knowledge products (the model card, the methodology and the data-source ledger) remain English-only, and where a sentence has no Bengali version the English one is shown rather than a gap.
bullets: An em dash (—), a value left blank, or the words “not reported” mean the run or the file did not supply that value. They never mean zero.
An unread file is not a count of zero, and no published alert is not the same as no hazard. The live strip states those cases separately, so a loading failure cannot be mistaken for safety.

If a panel cannot load, use its Try again button where one is offered, then check the status page to see whether the source file itself is stale or failing. The rest of the page stays readable while one panel is missing.
To report a broken page, a stale run or a prediction that looks wrong, use the contact page and include the district and the date: that is enough to act on.

sections.h2: The official record, and where it lives
paragraphs: HazardNet does not issue warnings, cyclone signals or evacuation instructions, and it must never be read as doing so. The bodies that do are named below; their bulletins outrank anything on this site.
bullets: Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD): weather forecasts, cyclone signals, and heat, cold and storm warnings.
Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC): river-level forecasts and flood bulletins.
Department of Disaster Management (DDM), Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief: the Standing Orders on Disaster, relief and response.
In an emergency, call the national hotline 999, and follow your local administration’s instructions over anything published here.

paragraphs: The platform is maintained as a Master’s thesis project at Bangladesh Agricultural University, and it improves fastest where practitioners push back on it.
bullets: Use it in the field and report where it was wrong. A district, a date and what you observed is enough to act on.
Reuse the data: the download centre carries the forecast snapshot and the offline builds, and the code is MIT-licensed with the citation given on this page.
Report a broken page, a stale run or a prediction that looks wrong from the contact page: every report is read.

faqs.question: Is HazardNet an official warning service?
faqs.answer: No. It is independent decision support for agriculture. Official warnings come from the Bangladesh Meteorological Department for weather hazards, the Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre for river floods, and the Department of Disaster Management with your local administration for response. For an emergency, call 999. HazardNet is meant to give you more lead time to prepare, not to replace those authorities.

faqs.question: My district is at Watch, Warning or Severe. What should I do?
faqs.answer: Read the level for what it says. Watch means monitor, conditions are favourable for a hazard; Warning means prepare, a damaging event is plausible; Severe means act, an event is imminent or likely. Then check the authority that can actually direct action: the BMD or FFWC bulletin for that hazard and your local administration. HazardNet's tiers are decision support with lead time attached; they are not cyclone signals or evacuation instructions. For farm work, time the job with the lead time and confirm it locally. In an emergency, call 999.

faqs.question: Is the confidence value a probability?
faqs.answer: No. The confidence value is an uncalibrated model score (a softmax output), not a calibrated chance that the event will occur, and the site labels it as what it is. Read it beside the severity value and the forecast date, and use the validation scorecard, which states what its counts can and cannot support, to judge how much weight a record deserves.

faqs.question: How often is HazardNet updated, and how can I tell if it is stale?
faqs.answer: Forecasts are updated in daily runs, and each run publishes dated files. The strip under the headline states the alerts file's age at the moment you read it, every forecast record carries its forecast date, and the status page states each artifact's age against the limit (its SLO) it is held to, including when a source is stale or failing. If a date is older than you expected, believe the date, not the design.

faqs.question: Why is there no alert (or no value) for my district?
faqs.answer: Three different situations look alike and are kept apart. A run may have assessed your district and withheld the row from publication; a run may not have covered the district at all, in which case its page says so instead of borrowing a neighbour's number; or a file may simply have failed to load on your connection. None of the three is shown as zero, and none of them means there is no hazard. The live map shows the current outlooks, and the status page says which of the three you are looking at.

faqs.question: Is this page available in Bengali?
faqs.answer: Yes, the switch at the top of this page renders the front door's editorial copy and its controls in Bengali. Where a sentence has no Bengali version, the English one is shown rather than a gap: the English copy is the structural authority, so a translation can reword a page but cannot shorten or reorder one. The alert cards, the map and the district tables were translated first; the long-form knowledge products, the model card, the methodology and the data-source ledger, remain English-only.

faqs.question: How should I cite HazardNet?
faqs.answer: The author, supervisors and institution are given in the attribution block on this page, and the repository ships a CITATION.cff with the same facts in machine-readable form. The code is MIT-licensed; the third-party data behind it keeps its own terms, which the data sources page lists one dataset at a time.

faqs.question: Why is the training archive not published here?
faqs.answer: The model card reports a 2,931-event archive (2000–2025) assembled from third-party records whose own licences govern redistribution. Rather than ship a stale copy that pages would quote as current, the repository ships the loader and the district and season pages state that no archive is loaded. The claim stays a claim until a deployment loads the export.

sections.h2: বর্তমান পূর্বাভাস, এবং তা কোথায় দেখবেন
paragraphs: এই পাতাটি দলিল; লাইভ মানচিত্র হলো পূর্বাভাস। এই বিভাজন ইচ্ছাকৃত ও নথিভুক্ত, কারণ দুটি প্রশ্নের জন্য দুই ধরনের পাতা দরকার: 'দুর্যোগ এখন কোথায়', এর উত্তর দেয় মানচিত্র; আর 'এটি কে তৈরি করেছে, কী থেকে তৈরি করেছে, এবং কাজ করা বন্ধ করলে আমি তা জানব কীভাবে', এর উত্তর দেয় তারিখ-সহ একটি দলিল।

শিরোনামের নিচের স্ট্রিপটি প্রতিবার লোড করলে সংরক্ষিত সতর্কবার্তা-আর্টিফ্যাক্ট পড়ে: প্রতিটি স্তরে কতটি সতর্কবার্তা প্রকাশিত, শেষ রান কতটি জেলা আওতা করেছে, এবং প্রকাশনা-গেট মূল্যায়িত কতটি সারি আটকে রেখেছে। কিছু প্রকাশিত না হলে সেটি স্পষ্ট করে বলা হয় এবং কারণও বলা হয়: দুর্যোগ প্ল্যাটফর্মে নীরবতাকে নিরাপত্তা বলে ধরে নেওয়া হয়, তাই এই পাতা সেটি অনুমানের ওপর ছেড়ে দেয় না।
bullets: লাইভ মানচিত্র ৬৪টি জেলার সবগুলোকেই আওতা করে। বর্তমান রানে যেসব জেলার তথ্য নেই, সেগুলো স্থির ভিত্তিমান রঙেই থাকে এবং নিজের পাতায় তা জানিয়ে দেয়: পাশের জেলার সংখ্যা ধার নেয় না।

প্রকাশিত প্রতিটি সতর্কবার্তার সঙ্গে তার নিজস্ব প্রমাণ থাকে: স্তরের পেছনের চালকগুলো, প্রয়োগ হওয়া নীতির সংস্করণ, এবং এটি কোনো দায়িত্বরত কর্মকর্তা পর্যালোচনা করেছেন নাকি ইঞ্জিন স্বয়ংক্রিয়-প্রকাশের সীমার মধ্যে থেকে নিজে প্রকাশ করেছে।
স্ট্যাটাস পাতায় এই ডিপ্লয়মেন্টের প্রতিটি আর্টিফ্যাক্টের বয়স থাকে, যে SLO মেনে চলার কথা তার বিপরীতে মাপা, এবং প্রতিটি রান নিজের বিরুদ্ধে যেসব নোট জানায় তাও থাকে।

paragraphs: এই ডিপ্লয়মেন্ট যে তারিখ-সহ পণ্যগুলো প্রকাশ করে। পর্যালোচনার তারিখ হলো সেই তারিখ যা পাতাটি নিজেই বহন করে, ফলে একটি পুরনো পণ্যকে পুরনো বলেই চেনা যায়।

sections.h2: সরকারি নথি, এবং তা কোথায় আছে
paragraphs: HazardNet কোনো সতর্কবার্তা, ঘূর্ণিঝড় সংকেত বা আশ্রয়ণ-নির্দেশনা জারি করে না, এবং একে কখনোই তাই মনে করা যাবে না। যেসব সংস্থা এগুলো জারি করে তাদের নাম নিচে দেওয়া; তাদের বুলেটিন এই সাইটের যেকোনো কিছুর চেয়ে অগ্রাধিকার পাবে।
bullets: বাংলাদেশ আবহাওয়া অধিদপ্তর (BMD): আবহাওয়ার পূর্বাভাস, ঘূর্ণিঝড় সংকেত, এবং তাপ, শৈত ও ঝড় সম্পর্কিত সতর্কবার্তা।
প্লাবন পূর্বাভাস ও সতর্কীকরণ কেন্দ্র (FFWC): নদীর পানির স্তরের পূর্বাভাস ও বন্যা বুলেটিন।
দুর্যোগ ব্যবস্থাপনা অধিদপ্তর (DDM), দুর্যোগ ব্যবস্থাপনা ও ত্রাণ মন্ত্রণালয়: দুর্যোগ বিষয়ক স্থায়ী আদেশ (Standing Orders on Disaster), ত্রাণ ও সাড়াদান।
জরুরি অবস্থায় জাতীয় হটলাইন ৯৯৯ নম্বরে কল করুন, এবং এখানে প্রকাশিত যেকোনো কিছুর চেয়ে আপনার স্থানীয় প্রশাসনের নির্দেশনা মেনে চলুন।

paragraphs: এই প্ল্যাটফর্মটি বাংলাদেশ কৃষি বিশ্ববিদ্যালয়ের এক এমএস থিসিস প্রকল্প হিসেবে রক্ষণাবেক্ষণ করা হয়, এবং অনুশীলনকারীরা এর সমালোচনা করলেই এটি সবচেয়ে দ্রুত উন্নত হয়।
bullets: মাঠে ব্যবহার করুন এবং কোথায় ভুল ছিল তা জানান। একটি জেলা, একটি তারিখ আর আপনি কী প্রত্যক্ষ করেছেন: কাজ করার জন্য এটুকুই যথেষ্ট।
তথ্য পুনর্ব্যবহার করুন: ডাউনলোড সেন্টারে পূর্বাভাস স্ন্যাপশট ও অফলাইন বিল্ড আছে, এবং কোড MIT লাইসেন্সযুক্ত: এই পাতায় উদ্ধৃতি দেওয়া আছে।
কোনো পাতা ভাঙা, রান পুরনো বা পূর্বাভাস ভুল মনে হলে যোগাযোগ পাতা থেকে জানান: প্রতিটি রিপোর্ট পড়া হয়।

faqs.question: HazardNet কি কোনো সরকারি সতর্কবার্তা সেবা?
faqs.answer: না। এটি কৃষির জন্য স্বাধীন সিদ্ধান্ত সহায়তা। সরকারি সতর্কবার্তা আসে আবহাওয়া-জনিত দুর্যোগের ক্ষেত্রে বাংলাদেশ আবহাওয়া অধিদপ্তর থেকে, নদীর বন্যার ক্ষেত্রে প্লাবন পূর্বাভাস ও সতর্কীকরণ কেন্দ্র (FFWC) থেকে, এবং সাড়াদানের ক্ষেত্রে দুর্যোগ ব্যবস্থাপনা অধিদপ্তর ও আপনার স্থানীয় প্রশাসন থেকে। জরুরি অবস্থায় ৯৯৯ নম্বরে কল করুন। HazardNet-এর উদ্দেশ্য প্রস্তুতির জন্য আপনাকে বেশি অগ্রিম সময় দেওয়া, ওই কর্তৃপক্ষগুলোর বিকল্প হওয়া নয়।

faqs.question: এই পাতা কি বাংলায় পাওয়া যায়?
faqs.answer: হ্যাঁ, এই পাতার ওপরের সুইচ ব্যবহার করলে সম্মুখপৃষ্ঠার সম্পাদকীয় লেখা ও নিয়ন্ত্রণগুলো বাংলায় দেখা যাবে। কোনো বাক্যের বাংলা সংস্করণ না থাকলে ফাঁকা না রেখে ইংরেজিটিই দেখানো হয়: ইংরেজি লেখাটিই কাঠামোগত ভিত্তি, তাই অনুবাদ একটি পাতাকে নতুন করে লিখতে পারে কিন্তু সংক্ষিপ্ত বা এলোমেলো করতে পারে না। সতর্কবার্তা কার্ড, মানচিত্র ও জেলার তালিকা আগেই অনূদিত হয���েছে; বিস্তারিত জ্ঞান-পণ্য, মডেল কার্ড, পদ্ধতি ও তথ্যসূত্র খতিয়ান, এখনো ইংরেজিতেই আছে।

faqs.question: HazardNet কীভাবে উদ্ধৃত করব?
faqs.answer: লেখক, তত্ত্বাবধায়ক ও প্রতিষ্ঠানের নাম এই পাতার স্বীকৃতি-অংশে দেওয়া আছে, এবং একই তথ্য মেশিন-পাঠযোগ্য রূপে CITATION.cff ফাইলে রিপোজিটরিতে আছে। কোড MIT লাইসেন্সযুক্ত; এর পেছনের তৃতীয় পক্ষের তথ্যের নিজস্ব শর্ত বহাল থাকে, যা তথ্যসূত্র পাতায় একেকটি ডেটাসেট হিসেবে তালিকাভুক্ত।

faqs.question: প্রশিক্ষণ আর্কাইভ কেন এখানে প্রকাশ করা হয়নি?
faqs.answer: মডেল কার্ডে ২,৯৩১ ঘটনার একটি আর্কাইভের (২০০০–২০২৫) কথা বলা হয়েছে, যা তৃতীয় পক্ষের রেকর্ড থেকে সংকলিত এবং যার নিজস্ব লাইসেন্স পুনর্বিতরণ নিয়ন্ত্রণ করে। একটি পুরনো কপি রেখে দেওয়ার চেয়ে, যা পাতাগুলো হালনাগাদ হিসেবে উদ্ধৃত করত, এই রিপোজিটরি লোডারটি সরবরাহ করে, এবং জেলা ও মৌসুমের পাতাগুলো জানিয়ে দেয় যে কোনো আর্কাইভ লোড করা নেই। যতদিন না কোনো ডিপ্লয়মেন্ট এক্সপোর্টটি লোড করে, ততদিন দাবিটি দাবিই থাকে।

routes.label: Live map
routes.title: Live hazard map: continuous 15-day daily outlooks for Bangladesh’s 64 districts
routes.description: The HazardNet GIS console: district-level continuous 15-day daily hazard trajectory, 0–100 severity index, peak severe dates, confidence bin and physics cross-check on an offline-capable map, with the run date printed beside it.
routes.standfirst: HazardNet is a free, non-commercial early-warning platform for Bangladesh agriculture. It converts environmental observations and weather forecasts into continuous 15-day daily outlooks for eight climate hazards across all 64 districts, then shows them on a map that keeps working when the connection does not.

paragraphs: The interactive map at the top of this page colours each district by the peak-severity hazard across its continuous 15-day daily outlook, where the latest model run covers it; districts outside that run keep their static baseline colour, and the district card in the dashboard states which of the two is shown. Selecting a district opens its forecast card: hazard type, severity index, peak severe dates, confidence bin, the crops and land cover at risk, and a direct link into all 15 daily steps.

Every number on the map comes from the most recent forecast snapshot the platform holds. The snapshot's prediction date is printed next to the map: if that date is more than a few days old, treat the outlook as stale and read the banner that explains why.

sections.h2: How to read the numbers honestly
bullets: Severity index (0.00–1.00 normalized, 0–100 index) is the model's continuous damage-potential score across Days 1 to 15. It is not a probability and not a percentage of damage.

Confidence (Certain ≥ 0.85, Probable 0.70–0.85, Uncertain < 0.70) is the model's own certainty in the hazard class it selected. It is not a measure of whether the forecast is correct, and it is not derived from the physics cross-check: the two tracks are computed separately and can disagree, and each district card shows both side by side so the divergence is visible.

Physics severity is an independent, formula-based estimate (for example, a vegetation-health index for drought or an excess-heat factor for heat waves). Model and physics severity diverging is normal and is shown rather than hidden.

Lead time spans a continuous 15-day daily trajectory (Days 1 to 15), with peak severe dates highlighted and a day picker to inspect any individual forecast day. Later days carry higher uncertainty; treat the entire trajectory as a planning window, not an official warning.

callout.text: HazardNet is decision support, not an official warning service. For evacuation, cyclone signals, flood bulletins and emergency instructions, follow the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD), the Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC) and your local administration.

paragraphs: Each figure is read from the published forecast record for the selected district and forecast date. How a record is generated is research-private.
A baseline colour is not an alert. For published warnings see the alerts surface; for the official record see the Bangladesh Meteorological Department and the Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre.

routes.label: Alerts
routes.title: Live hazard alerts for Bangladesh districts: HazardNet
routes.description: Published HazardNet alerts by district: level, hazard, continuous 15-day outlook window, the evidence behind each one, and the policy that decides it. Available in Bengali and English, and it keeps working offline.
routes.standfirst: Every alert HazardNet has published, district by district, with the evidence and the policy behind it. A watch is the highest level the engine can publish on its own; anything above a watch waits for a named duty officer to approve it. The list is rendered from live data, so this page also works from the snapshot the deployment carries when the API cannot be reached.

paragraphs: Four levels are published: no alert, watch, warning and severe. The level comes from the alert policy in force, at or below the configured ceiling for each hazard class, and is never inflated by this site.
Each alert states the hazard class, the district, the forecast window within the 15-day trajectory, the forecast issue time, the data cutoff and the model version it came from.

Every alert carries a model severity, an independently computed physics severity and the divergence between the two tracks. When the tracks disagree beyond the policy threshold the alert is flagged rather than silently averaged.

The score on a record is a relative priority signal for the class it carries. It is not a probability that the hazard will occur, and it is uncalibrated. The evidence behind an alert is the published forecast record itself: district, hazard, severity and forecast date.

The engine publishes at or below the watch level automatically. A warning or severe alert requires a named duty officer, a review timestamp and the model version and data cutoff recorded against the decision, so a published alert can always be traced back to the run that produced it.

Alerts are also delivered by SMS and Telegram to subscribers who have opted in. Both channels carry the same disclaimer as this page, and a single SMS is capped at 70 Bengali characters per segment, which is why the message body is short and links back to the evidence card.

routes.title: Methodology: how HazardNet builds a forecast
routes.description: What HazardNet publishes, records, severity values, horizons, freshness, validation status, and where the limits are.
routes.standfirst: Everything HazardNet does between a satellite pass and the district card on your screen, including the parts that are uncertain, delayed or not yet validated. If you are going to make a decision with this platform, this page is the one to read.

paragraphs: Each daily forecast run publishes a continuous 15-day sequence (Days 1 to 15) per district: dominant hazard class, continuous severity index (0 to 100), peak severe dates, and confidence score, stamped with the forecast date of the run that produced it.
bullets: Continuous 15-day daily outlooks for all 64 districts and eight hazard classes.
A severity value in two tracks, a skill track and a physics track, each labelled honestly.
Published alert levels where an alert policy applies.
A validation scorecard and a live freshness record.

sections.h2: 2 · How to read a severity value
paragraphs: Severity is a continuous value with two tracks reported side by side. The skill track is the system's own score for the class it selected; the physics track is an independent estimate. They can disagree, and when they do, that is shown rather than smoothed away. Confidence scores are uncalibrated.

Outlooks are published as a continuous 15-day daily trajectory (Days 1 to 15) per district, with peak severe dates highlighted across the full sequence. Every step is a planning window, not an official warning, and Days 8 to 15 carry greater meteorological uncertainty than Days 1 to 7.
Every surface shows the forecast date behind it. A stale run is labelled as stale; a missing run is shown as missing: no number is interpolated to fill a gap.

sections.h2: 5 · What is validated: and what is not
paragraphs: Forecast skill is not yet validated against observed outcomes. The published scorecard reports detection counts for five historical episodes and states what those numbers cannot support. No calibration accuracy is claimed.

Model code, dataset collection procedures, training and benchmarking are research-private. Only results and outputs are published: on this site and in the public repository. For research collaboration or licensing, use the contact page.

paragraphs: HazardNet publishes continuous 15-day daily multi-hazard outlooks for all 64 districts of Bangladesh: eight hazard classes, a continuous severity index (0 to 100), highlighted peak severe dates, and a confidence score per district and forecast date across Days 1 to 15.

paragraphs: Decision support for agricultural preparedness: more lead time to prepare fields, livestock and labour before a hazard window. Every figure is a planning input, not an order.

sections.h2: Out of scope: do not use it for this
paragraphs: Not an official warning. Not evacuation guidance. Not insurance or credit assessment. Not a metre-scale flood map. Not validated for any use where a wrong number causes harm on its own.

Fast-onset events can outrun the forecast window. A missing run is shown as missing. Confidence scores are uncalibrated and can be high while the class is wrong: treat the two severity tracks as signals to check, not as truth.
Coverage is uniform across the 64 districts. The site needs no account for the map and forecasts. Location, if you enable it, is used on your device and is never uploaded.

sections.h2: Reporting a problem with a prediction
paragraphs: Send the district, hazard, horizon and forecast date with what you observed on the ground, through the contact page. Ground-truth reports are how published skill metrics get built.

faqs.question: Is HazardNet an official government warning service?
faqs.answer: No. HazardNet is an independent, non-commercial decision-support platform. Cyclone signals, flood bulletins, evacuation orders and emergency instructions are issued by the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD), the Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC), the Department of Disaster Management (DDM) and your local administration. Always follow them over anything shown here. The national emergency hotline is 999.

faqs.question: What does the percentage next to a district actually mean?
faqs.answer: It is the model's severity index, scaled 0–100 for display. It is a continuous score of damage potential for the forecast unit and horizon: not a probability, and not a forecast that X% of the district will be damaged. The underlying value runs from 0.00 to 1.00 and is shown with the physics-based severity estimate beside it.

faqs.question: What is the difference between severity, confidence and physics severity?
faqs.answer: Severity is the model's damage-potential score. Physics severity is a formula-based estimate (for example a rainfall threshold for flood, an excess-heat factor for heat waves). Records published before 17 September 2026 computed it only for the hazard class the model selected, so it checked the model's magnitude rather than its choice of hazard; from that date all eight hazard classes are scored from the weather drivers alone and the class the physics track would have picked is published beside the model's. Confidence is the model's own certainty in that class: Certain at 0.85 and above, Probable between 0.70 and 0.85, Uncertain below 0.70. It does not measure agreement between the two tracks; when they diverge, both values stay visible on the card and the outlook should be treated as a question to verify rather than an alarm.

faqs.question: How fresh is the data, and how often is it updated?
faqs.answer: A refresh is attempted hourly and the published result is a committed snapshot. The prediction date is printed next to the map, and that date, not the time you opened the page, tells you how old the outlook is. If the pipeline fails, the site keeps serving the last good snapshot and labels its age rather than showing nothing.

faqs.question: Which hazards and which areas are covered?
faqs.answer: Eight hazards: cold wave, drought, fire, flash flood, flood, heat wave, severe local storm and tropical cyclone. The interactive map covers all 64 districts of Bangladesh, and the published archive covers 507 sub-district (ADM3) units, 495 upazilas plus 12 city corporations, using HDX COD-AB boundaries.

faqs.question: How far ahead can it really see?
faqs.answer: HazardNet publishes continuous 15-day daily outlooks (Days 1 to 15) across all 64 districts, driven by the deterministic weather forecast window (Open-Meteo serves up to 16 days). Each district page shows all 15 consecutive days, a 0 to 100 severity index, and highlighted peak severe dates. They are honest planning aids for seasonal decisions (irrigation, planting, stock movement), not storm-specific long-range warnings: read Days 8 to 15 as carrying higher uncertainty than Days 1 to 7.

faqs.question: Does HazardNet work offline?
faqs.answer: Partly, and the limits are worth knowing. The app installs as a PWA and caches map tiles you have already viewed, so previously visited areas can render without a connection. New forecasts, new areas and any export you have not generated before need a connection. Cached tiles are held in browser storage with a size cap, so a long time offline, or clearing site data, will empty the cache.

faqs.question: What exactly does a map or PDF export contain?
faqs.answer: The export captures the current view: the layers you have enabled, the district or region in frame, the prediction date, the legend, data attribution and the disclaimer. Resolution and page size are chosen in the export dialog before the file is generated, and the dialog states what will be in the filename, format and date range.

faqs.question: What happens to my data if I create an account?
faqs.answer: An account stores the profile fields you fill in, your saved districts, your connectors and your preferences so the dashboard can show them to you. Environmental forecasts do not depend on your account, and no personal data is used as model input. See the privacy policy for retention and deletion.

faqs.question: A district card looks wrong. What should I do?
faqs.answer: Send it in: district, hazard, horizon, date and what you observed on the ground. Ground-truth reports are the only route by which the platform can publish skill metrics, and they are how thresholds get corrected. Use the contact page, which reaches the maintainers directly.

A build script turns them into one artifact, served at /data/freshness.json: that is what this page renders, and what a script or a monitoring system can read.
The derived timestamp printed above each table is when that artifact was produced. It moves when the pipeline commits new data, when the probe commits a new result, and when the site is rebuilt.

bullets: Within SLO: the source is present and its age is inside the SLO that applies to it: 192 hours for the forecast data, 48 hours for the alert snapshot, 2 hours for the probe result.
Past SLO: the source is present but older than its SLO. The age and the SLO are both printed so the gap can be read directly.
Checks failing: the last site-health probe run reported at least one failed check; the checks table names them.
No data: the artifact the source describes is not present in this deployment at all. No age is printed, because there is nothing to age.

Unknown: the artifact could not be read, or it does not carry the timestamp the age would need. Unknown is a distinct state from No data on purpose: one means the file is missing, the other means we cannot tell.

sections.h2: What this page deliberately does not claim
bullets: It is not an uptime or availability report. No uptime history is kept and no percentage is computed here; the site-health probe reports an outcome per check, per run, and that is what it says.
It is not a live probe. A source can be Within SLO here while the deployed site is failing its checks: the probe row, not the freshness rows, is the live-surface signal.

It does not name missing districts when the run did not report them. The coverage stamp says how many districts the run covered; if the run did not list which ones are absent, this page says so rather than inferring them.

It does not describe a model version that does not exist. While the ingest pipeline does not stamp a model_version, the provenance row says Not stamped, and the alert engine's publication gate stays closed for everything above WATCH.
It is not an official warning service. Read the methodology page for scope, and heed the warnings issued by BMD, FFWC, DDM and your local administration.

callout.text: Within SLO on this page describes the committed data files the deployment ships, not the services that serve them. For the live surface, the homepage, deep links, security headers, the sitemap and the forecast endpoint, read the last site-health probe result in the table above or the Site Health Probe workflow run it links to.

faqs.question: How often is this page updated?
faqs.answer: Whenever the data it describes is committed: the scheduled forecast pipeline commits a new snapshot (and therefore a new derived artifact) when it runs, the site-health probe commits its result every 30 minutes on the default branch, and every deployment rebuilds the page from whatever artifact is committed at that commit. The derived timestamp printed with the tables is the authoritative answer for the copy you are reading.

faqs.question: Why does the model version say Not stamped?
faqs.answer: Because the ingest pipeline does not currently record a model_version on the rows it publishes, and this page will not print one it cannot prove. The same absence is why nothing above the WATCH level can be published automatically yet: the product spec requires a model version on a published alert, and the engine records that as a blocker instead of issuing one.

faqs.question: The alert list is empty: is that an error?
faqs.answer: No. The alert engine assessed the current run's rows and published none of them, because none of them had the model provenance a published alert requires. The count of assessed rows that produced no published alert is stated in the notes above, so an empty list is visible as a state rather than as a silent absence.

faqs.question: Does Within SLO mean the site is up?
faqs.answer: No. Within SLO is a statement about the age of a data file against its threshold. Whether the deployed site serves its pages, its headers and its API is what the site-health probe checks, and its result is reported separately above.

faqs.question: Does a severity value of 30 mean a 30 percent chance of an event?

faqs.question: Can I infer a historical risk trend from the yearly chart?

faqs.answer: The historical cleaned catalog has constant severity values and zero validated-affected values. Pearson correlation requires variation in both variables, so those correlations are undefined rather than zero.

paragraphs: A daily advisory row identifies a district, target date and selected hazard class. It carries a normalized severity score and meteorological fields where available. Forecast API records may also carry a confidence score and confidence_kind; some daily snapshot artifacts expose metrics.probTop1 without a separate confidence-kind field. bullets: District: one of the 64 districts of Bangladesh.
Target date and horizon: one of 15 consecutive daily steps, Days 1 to 15.
Hazard class: the selected class from the eight-class set.
Severity: a continuous normalized value from 0.00 to 1.00, shown as a 0 to 100 display index.
Confidence: a top-class score when present; only treat it as a calibrated probability when the source explicitly labels confidence_kind as calibrated_probability.
Run provenance: source version, model version and generated time identify the output snapshot.

paragraphs: Severity is reported side by side in two tracks. The model track is the system’s own score for its selected class; it is not a verification metric or an estimate of forecast skill. The physics track is an independent estimate built from the meteorological drivers alone. The two can disagree, and when they do, the disagreement is shown rather than smoothed away. Neither track is an official warning level.
Each daily run publishes 15 consecutive daily steps (Days 1 to 15) for each of the 64 districts (960 daily records total), highlighting the peak severe date or dates across the window.
Every surface is stamped with the forecast date behind it. A stale run is labelled as stale. A missing run is shown as missing. No number is interpolated to fill a gap.

formulas.label: Population standard deviation
formulas.spoken: Take the square root of the mean squared deviation from the mean.

formulas.label: Display index
formulas.spoken: Multiply normalized severity S by one hundred for the display index I.

formulas.label: Interquartile range and Tukey fences
formulas.expression: IQR = Q3 − Q1; fences = [Q1 − 1.5 × IQR, Q3 + 1.5 × IQR]
formulas.spoken: Interquartile range equals the third quartile minus the first quartile; Tukey fences extend one point five interquartile ranges on either side.
formulas.explanation: These are descriptive distribution diagnostics, not hazard thresholds. Here IQR is zero and all equal values lie on the fences.

formulas.label: Coefficient of variation
formulas.spoken: Coefficient of variation equals one hundred times population standard deviation divided by the absolute mean.
formulas.explanation: It is zero here because σ = 0 and μ = 0.30. It is undefined when the mean is zero.

formulas.label: Population skewness
formulas.spoken: Population skewness is the third central moment divided by the cube of the population standard deviation.
formulas.explanation: It is undefined when σ = 0. The published report correctly labels skewness undefined for this constant score set.

formulas.label: Pearson correlation
formulas.expression: rₓᵧ = Σ((xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ)) / √(Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)²)

routes.title: Validation status of HazardNet forecasts
routes.description: HazardNet forecast skill is not yet validated against observed outcomes. This page states what the published scorecard covers and what it cannot support, and what is not published.
routes.standfirst: What has been checked, what has not, and what stays research-private.

paragraphs: Forecast skill is not yet validated against observed outcomes. What is published today is a scorecard of per-episode detection counts, together with an explicit statement of what those numbers cannot support.
The scorecard reports detection counts for five historical episodes at an alarm threshold of 0.500 on the class severity score:
bullets: Cyclone Amphan: Bangladesh landfall, 20 May 2020.
Cyclone Yaas: Bangladesh coast, 26 May 2021.
Cyclone Mocha: Cox's Bazar coast and Teknaf, 14 May 2023.
Eastern flash floods: Feni, Cumilla and Noakhali, 20 to 30 August 2024.
Northeast and coastal monsoon floods: Sylhet, Sunamganj and the hill districts, from 1 June 2025.

callout.text: These are artifact totals, not a validated forecast-skill estimate. In particular, an alarm without a recorded impact is not automatically a false alarm: the outcome may be missing or unobserved.

paragraphs: The counts do not establish probability calibration, skill against a climatology baseline, or a general operational false-alarm rate. The artifact contains episode-specific derived metrics, but their denominators depend on the recorded outcomes and are not comparable as a pooled estimate. Its 532 alarms without a recorded impact are not confirmed no-impact cases. Until evaluation against verified outcomes ships, treat every severity value as decision support only.

Model code, dataset collection procedures, training and benchmarking are research-private. Only results and outputs are public, on this site and in the repository. For research collaboration or licensing enquiries, use the contact page.

The formulas below are standard definitions, not a claim that the current scorecard has a valid pooled estimate. A denominator of zero or an unavailable outcome makes a metric undefined; it must not be printed as zero.

formulas.label: Probability of detection
formulas.spoken: Hits divided by hits plus misses.
formulas.explanation: Undefined when TP + FN is zero; an episode count is not a multi-season skill estimate.

formulas.label: False alarm ratio
formulas.spoken: False alarms divided by all forecast events.
formulas.explanation: Undefined when TP + FP is zero; does not describe event probability calibration.

formulas.label: Critical success index
formulas.spoken: Hits divided by the union of forecast and observed events.
formulas.explanation: Requires a documented event match rule and a nonzero denominator.

formulas.label: Confidence calibration
formulas.expression: Compare stated confidence with observed event frequency in reliability bins.
formulas.spoken: Calibration compares forecasts grouped by confidence with corresponding observed event frequencies.
formulas.explanation: The current publication makes no calibration claim and does not publish the full training or benchmarking process.

sections.h2: What the current five-episode scorecard can say
paragraphs: The public artifact counts detections for five selected historical episodes at a class severity threshold of 0.500. It is not a broad prospective evaluation: the classifier was not re-run for the evaluation, episode selection is small, and several aggregate skill quantities are not published.

sections.h2: What a future validation study would require
paragraphs: A defensible evaluation would lock the unit and event-matching rule before scoring, use genuinely out-of-time episodes, compare with a named reference forecast, and retain complete outcome denominators. Probability scores would be reported only after probability semantics and calibration are established.

rows: Out-of-time seasons or episodes not used to select or tune the model.
Avoids leakage from fitting or selecting on the same events.

Makes TP, FP and FN reproducible.

formulas.label: Brier score, if probabilities are validated
formulas.spoken: Brier score equals the average squared difference between forecast probability and binary outcome.
formulas.explanation: Use only when pᵢ is a probability for a clearly defined event and oᵢ is a verified zero-or-one outcome. The current HazardNet documentation makes no Brier-score claim.

formulas.label: Brier skill score, relative to a named baseline
formulas.spoken: Brier skill score equals one minus the model Brier score divided by the reference Brier score.
formulas.explanation: The reference must be stated and evaluated on the same cases. BSS is not currently estimated for HazardNet.

formulas.label: Block-bootstrap uncertainty
formulas.spoken: Block bootstrap standard error is the standard deviation of the metric across B resamples of whole events or seasons.
formulas.explanation: Resample dependent event or season blocks rather than treating every district-day row as independent. A valid interval still requires enough independent blocks; the current five episodes are insufficient for a broad claim.

callout.text: These are candidate evaluation methods, not results. No probability-calibration, Brier-score, Brier-skill-score or confidence-interval result is published here.

faqs.question: Has HazardNet forecast skill been validated against observed outcomes?
faqs.answer: Not yet. The public scorecard reports descriptive detection counts for five historical episodes and explicitly says they are inconclusive.

faqs.question: Why not calculate p-values or confidence intervals from the current scorecard?
faqs.answer: Five selected episodes are not a suitable independent sample for a general skill claim. The outcome matching and negative sample space also need to be well-defined.

faqs.question: What does a null metric mean?
faqs.answer: It means the metric is not estimable from the available numerator and denominator. Null is not zero and must not be interpreted as no skill or no events.

faqs.question: Are model code and benchmark details public?
faqs.answer: No. Model code, data collection, training and benchmarking details remain research-private; only selected results and public outputs are published.

faqs.question: What would be needed for a future forecast-skill claim?
faqs.answer: A pre-specified matching rule, independent out-of-time cases, complete outcome denominators, a named baseline, lead-time and hazard-specific reporting, and uncertainty methods that resample dependent events or seasons.
